AfriScan · Ghana · Secure your land from the air, remotely

See what has changed on your land and rights of way in Ghana

AfriScan maps structures, excavations, cleared ground and tracks along pipeline, power-line, rail and fibre corridors, and in and around mining leases across Ghana. We work from dated satellite imagery, from the drone imagery your own teams fly, or from drone surveys flown subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires. Each structure gets an ID, coordinates and a distance to your line or boundary, and a person checks the results before they reach you, as GIS files and a PDF report your land, safety and community-relations teams can use.

The rules behind the record Minerals and Mining Act 2006 (Act 703) s.72 · L.I. 2175 compensation and resettlement · L.I. 542 as amended by L.I. 1737 · Environmental Assessment Regulations 2025 (L.I. 2504) · GCAD Part 28 · Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) · IFC Performance Standard 5

Already in Ghana's law

Lines on the map that only mean something if you can see the ground

Ghanaian law draws protected strips along power lines, needs the lease holder’s consent for new buildings in a mining area and fixes compensation to a cut-off date. Each of those rules depends on a record of what stood where, and when.

L.I. 542, as amended by L.I. 1737

Power lines: protected strips either side

The transmission-line protection regulations bar drilling, excavation, lorry parks, shops, garages, barns and real-estate development within 15 m either side of the centre of a 161 kV line and 20 m of a 330 kV line, as GRIDCo described them in September 2026. You can only plan for what you can see on the ground.

Act 703, s.72(4)

Mining areas: building needs consent

Under the Minerals and Mining Act, the owner or lawful occupier of land in a mining area “shall not erect a building or a structure without the consent of the holder of the mining lease”. A dated record shows what stood there, and from when.

L.I. 2175, regs 1(8) and 16

Compensation: fixed to a cut-off date

Ghana’s mining compensation regulations use a cut-off date published in the district, and treat “speculative development” after it differently. A structure inventory on that date supports fair, transparent compensation.

Why it matters

What changes between visits

Ghana’s pipelines, transmission lines and mining leases sit among farms, towns, rivers and forest reserves. The ground beside them changes faster than any inspection cycle can write down.

“New structures keep appearing under the line.”

Kiosks, sheds, workshops and houses go up inside protected strips, most often where a line runs beside a road or a town grows towards it. Each one is easier to plan for, and to discuss, while it is new and few.

“The ground has been dug up near our boundary.”

Galamsey pits, washing sites, spoil and cleared ground can open up inside a lease, at its edge or close to a buried pipeline or cable. Imagery shows where and when the land changed; your team decides what happens next.

“We need a record before the new route is fixed.”

A new pipeline, line or road starts with route options and an environmental permit application. A dated count of the structures along each option, taken before the investment decision, is the record later discussions go back to.

“The cut-off date is coming.”

When a mining lease expands, a new line is acquired or a resettlement plan starts, the structures standing on the cut-off date decide who is compensated for what. The census teams need to know where to go.

What you receive

A register your land, safety and GIS teams can open straight away

  • A structure inventory: each structure with an ID, its distance to the line or boundary, its band, its chainage and its coordinates in WGS84 and in the route’s UTM zone (30N or 31N in Ghana).
  • Counts by band: how many structures stand inside the protected strip or corridor, and in the wider bands you choose.
  • Change since the last survey: new and removed structures, fresh excavations, cleared ground and new tracks, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer.
  • Every 500 m rated high, medium or low by how many structures stand near the line, so the team knows where to start.
  • A PDF report and GIS layers in GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile, and an interactive map file that opens in a browser, including in the field.

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations, tracks and changes in vegetation and water. We do not identify, count or follow people, and whether a structure or a working is authorised is for you and the authorities to decide. Our work is land and environmental mapping for the holder of the asset, not a security or enforcement service.

A person reviews the results

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds. What the imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

Dated and credited

Each report names its imagery and, where the source gives one, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled re-surveys

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, never a promise of constant watching, with a notice of what changed and where.

Confidential by default

Results go only to the contacts you name, and nothing about your assets is published. Registers record structures and coordinates, not names.

Satellite first, drones where the approvals allow

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route or lease file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos your own drone teams already fly. Satellite-based screening needs no drone permit, because nothing flies, and it covers a whole corridor before anyone decides where a team should go.

Drone detail. Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite imagery shows, a drone survey captures it, subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires. In Ghana, commercial drone work needs an RPAS Operator Certificate that only a company registered in Ghana can obtain, registered drones with permits, and pilots with remote pilot licences. The GCAA and the Ministry of National Security have set no-fly zones around security facilities, airports, power stations and ports, flights within 30 m of buildings, vehicles or groups of people need explicit permission, and work near high-tension wires needs a special authorisation. Afridrone is working towards the authorisations Ghana requires, and every drone proposal lists the approvals its flights need.

For procurement and compliance teams

Local content, supplier registration and data protection

Mining contracts in Ghana follow the Minerals Commission’s Local Procurement List, which reserves “Geophysical Ground-based Survey; Mapping, Pitting and Trenching” (item 35) to firms incorporated in Ghana with exclusively Ghanaian directors and shareholders; whether that reaches remote satellite analysis is a question for counsel. Upstream petroleum service companies need a Petroleum Commission permit, public buyers procure through GHANEPS, and organisations that process personal data register with the Data Protection Commission. Our notes set out what each rule means for mapping and drone work, and what to ask any supplier for.

Working with AfriScan in Ghana

We respond to tenders, RFQs and requests for proposals. Send your supplier or prequalification forms with your request; the proposal names the company that holds each registration your contract needs, and the Ghanaian firm that holds the contract where local-content rules require one.

How we work · Send tender documents

Where we send people

Remote first, and field work only where it is safe

Most of our work in Ghana needs no one on site. Where a ground check or a drone flight is planned, we do not send field teams or fly in the areas covered by the UK and US governments’ travel warnings: the Bawku Municipal area and the North East Region; the Nasia–Walewale–Bolgatanga and Bolgatanga–Zebilla–Bawku–Pulmankom roads and their corridors, which the UK advice names; the northern border areas of the Upper East and Upper West regions; and the Savannah Region west of the N12. Nor do we send crews or drones to sites where enforcement operations are under way.

Ask about satellite-only work

If your asset runs through one of these areas, tell us in your request. What can be done from imagery alone is agreed project by project.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure in Ghana?

The ones that apply to your asset. For 161 kV and 330 kV transmission lines we report the protected strips of 15 m and 20 m either side of the centre of the line, as GRIDCo describes the transmission-line protection regulations. For pipelines we measure from the centreline you send, or from the corridor boundary if you send it as a polygon, to the width in your acquisition instrument, wayleave or company standard. For a mining lease we work from the boundary you give us, with a ring around it. Wider reporting bands, such as 50, 100 and 200 m, can be added to any of these.

Do you need anyone on site to start?

No. A survey starts from your route or boundary file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold, so nobody travels and no drone flies. That matters where access is difficult or unsafe. Drone detail is added only where a stretch needs it, subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires.

Does this replace right-of-way patrols or lease inspections?

No. It tells your patrol, land and community teams where the ground has changed since the last survey, so they go there first, and it gives them a dated record to take with them.

Can you tell us who built a structure or who is digging?

No. We map the land, not people. The register records a structure, a pit or a patch of cleared ground, where it is and on which imagery date it first appears. It never identifies, counts or follows anyone, and whether a structure or a working is authorised is for you and the authorities to decide.

Can the register be shared with chiefs, the District Assembly or the people along the line?

That is your decision. A neutral, dated map of what stood where is often the starting point for engagement with traditional authorities and communities, for compensation processes and for grievance handling. We never publish maps of your assets or of the settlements around them without your written permission.

Do you work through Ghanaian firms?

Where the rules call for it, yes. On mining leases, item 35 of the Minerals Commission’s Local Procurement List, “Geophysical Ground-based Survey; Mapping, Pitting and Trenching”, is reserved to firms incorporated in Ghana with exclusively Ghanaian directors and shareholders. Whether it reaches remote satellite analysis is a question for counsel, so AfriScan works there as the technology supplier to a qualifying Ghanaian firm, which holds the contract. Where your own survey team already flies drones, we run our analysis on its imagery. Working with AfriScan in Ghana sets out the rules.

Know what stands on your right of way or lease, and since when.

Send the route or lease boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the regions and districts it crosses, and the widths that matter: the protected strip for the line's voltage, the corridor in your acquisition instrument or wayleave, or your company standard. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
